title: The Debye Function is Used to Calculate the Heat Capacity at Low Temperatures
lead: Near absolute zero the heat capacity of a solid falls far below the Dulong–Petit value. Debye's model of the lattice vibrations as phonons gives its form at low temperature, and in a metal the conduction electrons add a term of their own.
exercise_notes: The book sets no exercise for this section; the one exercise, on extending the T³ law and the entropy below the lowest measured temperature, was written by AI with an AI solution. Its Bloom level and concept tags were chosen by AI. Numeric answers accept a 2% tolerance.

exercises.prompt: At low temperature the heat capacity of a nonmetallic crystal follows Equation 21.4.1, $\kCP = \ka\kT^3$, and at 5.0 K it is 0.10 J/(mol K). (a) What is $\kCP$ at 10.0 K? (b) Taking $\kSent = 0$ at 0 K, what is the molar entropy of the crystal at 10.0 K?

answer.solution: (a) $\ka = 0.10/(5.0)^3 = 8.0\times10^{-4}$ J mol⁻¹ K⁻⁴, so at 10.0 K $\kCP = (8.0\times10^{-4})(10.0)^3 = 0.80$ J/(mol K), eight times the value at 5.0 K. (b) $\kSent(\kT) = \displaystyle\int_0^{\kT}\dfrac{\ka\kT^3}{\kT}\,d\kT = \dfrac{\ka\kT^3}{3} = \dfrac{\kCP(\kT)}{3}$, so $\kSent(10.0\ \text{K}) = 0.80/3 = 0.267$ J/(mol K). This is how calorimetry fills in the stretch below its lowest measured temperature: the entropy there is a third of the heat capacity measured at that temperature.
